newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SOUTHERN AFRICAN MPS TO SCRUTINISE TRADE PACTS.
newsitem.headline: SOUTHERN AFRICAN MPS TO SCRUTINISE TRADE PACTS.

text.p: Four trade negotiations that could decisively shape the economic prospects of South Africa and its neighbouring states will come under the spotlight this weekend at a trade workshop for regional parliamentarians.

Parliamentary Speaker Frene Ginwala told a media briefing on Tuesday the four agreements would have significant implications for growth, employment and development in the 12 Southern African Development Community (SADC) states.
- the detailed negotiations on tariff reductions over the next eight years envisaged under the SADC free trade protocol adopted in August last year;
- the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) agreement covering South Africa, Botswana, Lesotho, Swaziland and Namibia, which was being re-negotiated;

- the Lome IV convention between the European Union (EU) and the African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) states. This did not affect South Africa directly as it had only partial accession to the convention but negotiations were due to start in Gabon in Nvember on a successor treaty, which was likely to be less favourable to ACP states.
- the negotiations on a free trade agreement between the EU and South Africa, which South Africa feared could have adverse implications for its neighbours.
Asked which of these agreements was of most immediate importance to South Africa, trade and industry committee chairman Rob Davies said he believed it was the SADC trade protocol.
The other SADC states - Botswana, Lesotho, Swaziland, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Angola, Zambia, Mauritius, Malawi, Namibia and Tanzania - were the main destination for South Africa exports.

"It is slightly larger than the EU and on top of that the kinds of products that we are sending into SADC are the kinds of products that we need to emphasise in terms of our economic development strategies - they are manufactured goods," Davies said.
"But if you look at our imports, these have remained remarkably flat so that the gap between our exports and imports has been widening.
"Part of the willingness to enter into the protocol has been a recognition that we have to address this question."
Next most important were the EU-South Africa negotiations, which were expected to get underway shortly.
"SACU is also important and, although it does not directly affect us, there is a clock ticking on the Lome negotiations and they have got great relevance for our neighbours," Davies said.
The workshop will be held in parliament on Friday and Saturday.
Seven parliamentarians from each country, with the possible exception of Angola, will attend the workshop along with local and international observers.
The workshop will be followed later in June by the first meeting of the SADC parliamentary forum.
